deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is part of Riemann's 1857 fragment on linear differential equations with algebraic coefficients, later printed in the Nachlass section of the Werke as 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten'. Riemann studies systems (y_1,…,y_n) of multivalued functions. Such a system has a finite set of branch points a, b, …, g. A closed loop around a branch point transforms the system by a constant linear substitution (A), (B), …, (G). At each branch point the system has exponents (characteristic exponents). A 'class' is the set of all systems with the same substitutions.

Results taken from the previous page:
(i) The derivative system (y_1', …, y_n') belongs to the same class.
(ii) Corollary 1: the y satisfy an n-th order linear ODE whose coefficients are polynomials.
(iii) Corollary 2: every system Y of the same class can be written as Y_i = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r_k(x) y_i^{(k)} with rational functions r_k. The r_k are the same for all i.

This page uses (iii) to find all systems that share both the substitutions and the exponents of y.

Step 1 (clearing denominators). Solve Y_i = sum r_k y_i^{(k)} by Cramer's rule. Here r_k = W_k/W, where W = det(y_i^{(j)}) is the Wronskian and W_k is W with column k replaced by Y. Multiplying through by a common polynomial denominator c_0 gives
  c_0 Y_i = b_0 y_i + b_1 y_i' + … + b_{n-1} y_i^{(n-1)},  i = 1..n,
with c_0 and the b_k polynomials in x.
- [My gloss] c_0 comes from W times the power factors (x-a)^{…}…(x-g)^{…} of the previous page. Hence it depends only on y, not on Y.
- [My gloss] Comparing growth at x = ∞ (the exponent condition at infinity) bounds the degrees of the b_k. So the b_k carry only finitely many unknown coefficients.

Step 2 (conditions). Y must have, at every branch point, exponents not lower than those of y. Y must also stay finite at every other point. This includes the zeros of c_0, which are generally apparent singularities of the right-hand side divided by c_0.
- The right-hand side is linear in the b_k.
- So these conditions are a finite homogeneous linear system for the polynomial coefficients of the b_k.

Step 3 (solution space). The solutions form a finite-dimensional vector space containing Y = y.
- If the linear equations fix the ratios of the unknowns, the space is 1-dimensional and Y = const·y.
- Otherwise the general solution is Y_i = k y_i + k_1 𝔜_i^{(1)} + … + k_m 𝔜_i^{(m)}, with arbitrary constants k, k_1, …, k_m. Here 𝔜^{(1)}, …, 𝔜^{(m)} are particular systems.

Step 4 (continued on the next page). The constants are fixed one at a time by requiring leading coefficients of the expansions of 𝔄^{-1}(y), … to vanish.
- Each such choice raises the exponent sum by at least 1.
- After m steps one obtains a system with raised exponents, unique up to a common constant factor, which is then normalized.
- This prepares the next page's study of how the normalized system depends on the position of a branch point a with the substitutions kept constant. That is isomonodromic deformation.
errors: In the displayed equations for c_0 Y_2 and c_0 Y_n, the image appears to show y_1' (first derivative of y_1) in the b_1 term instead of y_2' and y_n'. This is a scribal slip; by the context the i-th equation must involve only y_i and its derivatives.

The claim that c_0 depends only on y and that the degrees of the b_k are bounded is stated without proof. It follows from Cramer's rule with the Wronskian and from the exponent condition at infinity, so it is a justified but compressed step.
Grammatical slip in the transcription/manuscript: 'n linearer Gleichungen' should be 'n lineare Gleichungen'.

The condition 'Y finite at all other x' must include the zeros of c_0 (apparent singularities). Riemann does not mention this explicitly, but it is covered by his phrasing 'für alle anderen Werthe von x endlich bleiben'.

results.what: Every system with the same monodromy is a rational-coefficient combination of y and its first n-1 derivatives. After clearing denominators: c_0 Y = sum b_k y^(k) with polynomial b_k.
results.modern_name: Monodromy-preserving (contiguity/Schlesinger) transformations; gauge transformations by rational matrices preserving monodromy
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857 Nachlass, publ. 1876); generalizing Gauss's contiguous relations (1812); later Schlesinger

results.what: Systems with prescribed monodromy and exponents are found by solving a finite homogeneous linear system for polynomial coefficients. The space of solutions is finite-dimensional, Y = k y + sum k_i 𝔜^(i).
results.modern_name: Finite-dimensionality of the space of solutions with prescribed monodromy and bounded-below exponents (lattices/Riemann-Hilbert problem bookkeeping, parameter counting)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1857 fragment; systematized by Hilbert (21st problem), Plemelj, Birkhoff

results.what: Normalization by raising exponents to obtain a system unique up to a constant (continued on next page), leading to isomonodromic dependence on branch points.
results.usually_credited_to: Schlesinger (1905/1912), Fuchs R. (1905), Garnier; idea present in Riemann's fragment

deep.surprise_reason: The page belongs to Riemann's 1857 fragment 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten', published in his Werke (1876). Historians already credit him with this setup of the Riemann-Hilbert problem and the germ of isomonodromy. There is nothing beyond the published text.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x'); F=-log(1-x)/x; G=hyperexpand(hyper([2,1],[2],x)); simplify(1*(G-F) - x*diff(F,x))
checkable.asserts: Gauss contiguity a(F(a+1,b;c)-F(a,b;c)) = x F'(a,b;c) for a=b=1, c=2 (result 0). This is an instance of a system with the same monodromy and shifted exponents expressed linearly in y and y' with rational coefficients.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x'); a,b,c=Rational(1,3),Rational(1,4),Rational(1,2); F=hyper([a,b],[c],x); simplify(diff(F,x) - a*b/c*hyper([a+1,b+1],[c+1],x))
checkable.asserts: The derivative of a hypergeometric solution belongs to the same class: d/dx F(a,b;c;x) = (ab/c) F(a+1,b+1;c+1;x) (expected 0).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x'); y1,y2,Y=[Function(n)(x) for n in ('y1','y2','Y')]; W=y1*diff(y2,x)-y2*diff(y1,x); r0=(Y*diff(y2,x)-y2*diff(Y,x))/W; r1=(y1*diff(Y,x)-Y*diff(y1,x))/W; simplify(r0*y1+r1*diff(y1,x)-Y)
checkable.asserts: Cramer's rule for n=2 gives Y_1 = r0 y1 + r1 y1' with r_k = W_k/W (result 0 at the formal level; in the theory Y_2 is a second function and r0, r1 are single-valued, hence rational).

'n linearer Gleichungen' should read 'n lineare Gleichungen'.
In the second and last displayed equations the manuscript seems to write b_1 y_1' rather than b_1 y_2' and b_1 y_n'. The transcription silently corrects this; it is a slip in the original.

The marginal insertion 'Potenzen von x in den' at left belongs before 'Functionen b': 'für die Coefficienten der Potenzen von x in den Functionen b ein System linearer homogener Gleichungen'. The transcription handles this correctly.
